```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  render = function(x, ...) {
    if (inherits(x, "shiny.appobj")) invisible() else knitr::knit_print(x, ...)
  }
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(blockr.core)
library(blockr.dock)
library(blockr.assistant)
```

An app script of blockr.assistant 0.1 puts the assistant on a dock board, as an extension that `new_assistant_extension()` makes.
That assistant runs in the session's R process.
It calls its model through ellmer, and its tools change the board in R.
In version 0.2, the browser holds the board, as the migration notes of blockr.core describe (`vignette("migration-notes", package = "blockr.core")`).
The assistant is a plugin there, whose agent loop runs in the browser.
It calls its model from the browser too, and the board holds its conversations, as the state of its plugin.

These notes list each change that an app script needs to run the assistant of blockr.assistant 0.2.
They also list what changes for the deployment that serves the script, in its blockr options and its environment variables.
The last part lists what changes for the skills that a deployment gives the assistant.
The notes are written so that an AI can apply them.
Each section names what a script, a deployment or a skill uses in version 0.1, says what takes its place, and shows both versions.
A function of version 0.1 that is gone has no alias, so a script that still calls it stops with R's error that the function cannot be found.
An argument that is gone stops the call as an unused argument.
A blockr option that is gone is read by nothing, so a deployment that still sets it gets no error, and the value changes nothing.
A script follows the migration notes of blockr.core and blockr.dock too, and those of each other blockr package that it calls.

## The assistant's plugin

In version 0.1, a script puts the assistant on a dock board with `new_assistant_extension()`, in the `extensions` of `new_dock_board()`.
In version 0.2, the assistant is a plugin of the class `blockr.assistant-assistant_plugin`, which `new_assistant_plugin()` makes.
A script puts that plugin in the `plugins` of `new_board()`, under the name that the extension had:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
serve(
  new_dock_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris")),
    extensions = list(assistant = new_assistant_extension())
  )
)
```

```{r}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
serve(
  new_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris")),
    plugins = list(assistant = new_assistant_plugin())
  )
)
```

The function `serve()` runs the assistant even where the board holds no plugin of its class.
Its `plugins` default to every plugin class that `available_plugins()` lists.
That list holds the assistant's class wherever blockr.assistant is available.
The default is a convenience for interactive use.
A script does not rely on it, and puts the assistant's plugin on its board.
Where the app's plugins then lack the assistant's class, `serve()` stops and names the class, rather than serve the board without the assistant.

The dock adds a view to a board that has none, as the notes of blockr.dock say.
That view shows the assistant's panel on its left rail, beside the panels of the app's other plugins.

A script that places the assistant's panel in a grid names the panel with `plg()`, by the plugin's name in `plugins`, as the notes of blockr.dock say of every extension:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
board <- new_dock_board(
  blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
  links = new_link("a", "b"),
  extensions = list(assistant = new_assistant_extension()),
  views = list(main = list(blk("a"), blk("b"), ext("assistant"))),
  grids = list(
    main = dock_grid(
      panels("a", "b"),
      rail(ext("assistant"), position = "right")
    )
  )
)
```

```{r}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
board <- new_board(
  blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
  links = new_link("a", "b"),
  plugins = list(
    new_dock_plugin(
      views = list(
        main = dock_view(
          dock_grid(
            panels("a", "b"),
            rail(plg("assistant"), position = "right")
          )
        )
      )
    ),
    assistant = new_assistant_plugin()
  )
)
```

In version 0.1, an assistant without a name in `extensions` has the name `assistant`.
So a script gives the plugin of such an assistant that name too, as `assistant = new_assistant_plugin()` above.
A grid that placed its panel with `ext("assistant")` then places it with `plg("assistant")`.
A grid may also name the panel by the id of the plugin's class, as `plg("blockr.assistant-assistant_plugin")`.
Core's `new_board()` refuses a `plg()` whose id is neither a name in `plugins` nor the id of a plugin class.

The function `new_assistant_plugin(conversations = list())` takes the conversations of a board that a script builds.
Its `conversations` take the place of the `threads` of `new_assistant_extension()`.
Each conversation is a list under its id, with a `title`, the time it was `updated`, its `messages`, the tokens that it spent in `usage`, and its pick of the `model`, or `NULL` for the default (`?new_assistant_plugin`).
The records that version 0.1 took in `threads` do not carry over.
A script that gave some writes them again in this shape:

```{r}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
new_assistant_plugin(
  conversations = list(
    c1 = list(
      title = "Sales by region",
      updated = "2026-11-16T08:00:00Z",
      messages = list(
        list(
          id = "m1",
          role = "user",
          parts = list(list(type = "text", text = "Sum the sales by region.")),
          created = "2026-11-16T08:00:00Z"
        )
      ),
      usage = list(input = 0, output = 0, last = 0),
      model = NULL
    )
  )
)
```

The other arguments of `new_assistant_extension()` go too.
Its `system_prompt` gives way to a skill or a template ([The system prompt](#the-system-prompt)).
Its `...`, which it passed on to the `new_dock_extension()` of blockr.dock, has no counterpart, since `new_assistant_plugin()` takes the plugin's state alone.

In version 0.1, an app runs the assistant only where its script puts the assistant on the board.
In version 0.2, `serve()` runs it by default wherever blockr.assistant is available, as above.
So a script whose app should run no assistant leaves the assistant's row out of the plugins that `serve()` takes:

```{r}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
serve(
  new_board(),
  plugins = subset(available_plugins(), package != "blockr.assistant")
)
```

## The system prompt

In version 0.1, the `system_prompt` of `new_assistant_extension()` gives the system prompt.
It takes a function, `default_system_prompt()` by default, which R calls each time the board changes.
It also takes a string, which takes the place of the whole prompt.
In version 0.2, the plugin builds the system prompt in the browser, before each call to the model.
A function in R cannot shape that prompt, so `system_prompt` goes, and so does `default_system_prompt()`.

A script moves its own instructions to one of two places:

- A skill, in the directory that the blockr option `assistant_skills` names ([A deployment's skills](#a-deployments-skills)).
  The system prompt lists each skill that names no class, with its description, and the model reads a skill when the description says that it bears on the task.
  A skill suits instructions for one kind of task, such as building a clinical table.
- A template, a Markdown file that the blockr option `assistant_template` names.
  A template suits instructions for every call, such as who the assistant is and how it answers.
  It also suits instructions that change those of blockr.assistant, since a skill that contradicts them leaves the model two instructions to choose between.

A template takes the place of three sections of blockr.assistant's prompt, each with an id:

| Id | What the section tells the model |
|---|---|
| `role` | That it is an assistant next to a blockr data analysis board |
| `build` | To build what the user wants analysed, with defaults from the data, rather than ask first |
| `style` | To answer concisely |

The file names each section that it keeps as `<<id>>` on a line of its own, in the order in which the model reads them.
It may add text of its own around them, and it leaves out a section by not naming it.
So a script whose function of version 0.1 added text to the default prompt adds that text to a template:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
german <- function(board, client, ...) {
  paste(
    default_system_prompt(board, client, ...),
    "Answer in German.",
    sep = "\n\n"
  )
}

serve(
  new_dock_board(
    extensions = list(assistant = new_assistant_extension(system_prompt = german))
  )
)
```

In version 0.2, the template is a file beside the script, here `german.md`:

```markdown
<<role>>

<<build>>

<<style>>

Answer in German.
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
options(blockr.assistant_template = "german.md")

serve(new_board())
```

The plugin writes the rest of the prompt, whatever the template holds.
After the template, the system prompt holds blockr.assistant's rules, the app's plugins and the board options that its packages define, and the catalogue of skills.
After the conversation's last message, a message of the app's holds the board and what the user has on screen.
So a string that took the place of the whole prompt in version 0.1 has no counterpart.
Its text goes into a template or a skill, beside what the plugin writes.
A function that wrote the board into its prompt has no counterpart either, since the plugin tells the model the board before each call.
The section Template of `?new_assistant_plugin` lists every part of the prompt, in the order in which the model reads them.

As a board opens, the plugin has R read the template.
Where R cannot read the file, or where the file names an id that is none of the three, the plugin raises the error `assistant_template_failed`.
The calls then go on with blockr.assistant's own template until the next board opens.

## Where the calls go

In version 0.1, the assistant calls its model from the session's R process, through an ellmer chat.
The blockr option `chat_function` gives one of ellmer's chat functions, which fixes the model, or a named list of them.
From a list, the user picks one through the board option `llm_model` of blockr.core.
Where `chat_function` is unset, the chat is `ellmer::chat_openai()`, which reads its key from the environment variable `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

In version 0.2, the assistant calls its model from the browser, never through R.
Four blockr options say where the calls go, how they are authenticated and which models the assistant offers.
A deployment sets each as an R option, such as `blockr.assistant_models`, or as an environment variable, such as `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_MODELS`:

| Blockr option | What it holds | Where it is unset |
|---|---|---|
| `assistant_base_url` | The base URL that every call goes to | OpenAI's API, `https://api.openai.com/v1` |
| `assistant_api` | The API that the base URL speaks: `"openai-responses"` for OpenAI's Responses API, `"openai-completions"` for its Chat Completions API, or `"anthropic-messages"` for Anthropic's Messages API | `"openai-responses"` |
| `assistant_api_key` | The key that every call carries, or `"none"` for a base URL that needs no key | The chat asks each visitor for a key of their own |
| `assistant_models` | The ids of the models offered, the first being the default, as a character vector or as one string that separates them by commas | The models of the base URL's list that take tools, the first being the default |

The blockr option `chat_function` goes.
So does the board option `llm_model`, with its constructor `new_llm_model_option()`, which blockr.core no longer has.
A deployment moves to the four blockr options in these steps:

1. A deployment that gives the key in `OPENAI_API_KEY` sets it in `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_API_KEY` too.
   The assistant reads no variable of a provider's own clients.
   Without `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_API_KEY`, the chat asks each visitor for a key of their own.
2. A script that sets `chat_function` drops it.
   It names the models of the list's entries in `assistant_models`, in the same order, so that the first stays the default.
3. A deployment that leaves `chat_function` unset names the model that it chats with in `assistant_models`.
   Otherwise, the assistant offers each model of OpenAI's list that takes tools.
   That list follows no documented order, so the default could be any of them.
4. A chat function of another provider becomes that provider's base URL in `assistant_base_url`.
   The deployment sets `assistant_api` too, where the base URL does not speak OpenAI's Responses API.
   The provider's key goes in `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_API_KEY`, as in step 1.

A deployment of OpenAI's models thus keeps its key, and names its models:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
chat_with <- function(model) {
  force(model)
  function(system_prompt = NULL, params = NULL) {
    ellmer::chat_openai(
      model = model,
      system_prompt = system_prompt,
      params = params
    )
  }
}

models <- c("gpt-5.4", "gpt-5.4-nano")

options(
  blockr.chat_function = stats::setNames(lapply(models, chat_with), models)
)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
options(blockr.assistant_models = c("gpt-5.4", "gpt-5.4-nano"))
```

Its environment then holds `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_API_KEY`, with the key that `OPENAI_API_KEY` holds.
A deployment that sets its blockr options in its environment alone, as on Posit Connect, sets `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_MODELS=gpt-5.4,gpt-5.4-nano` in place of the R option.

A deployment of Anthropic's models names Anthropic's base URL and API:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
options(
  blockr.chat_function = function(system_prompt = NULL, params = NULL) {
    ellmer::chat_anthropic(
      model = "claude-sonnet-5-5",
      system_prompt = system_prompt,
      params = params
    )
  }
)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
options(
  blockr.assistant_base_url = "https://api.anthropic.com",
  blockr.assistant_api = "anthropic-messages",
  blockr.assistant_models = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
)
```

The key that `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` holds goes in `BLOCKR_ASSISTANT_API_KEY`.
Anthropic's base URL has no `/v1`, since the assistant appends `/v1/messages` to it.

Each argument of an ellmer chat function goes as follows:

| Version 0.1 | Version 0.2 |
|---|---|
| `model` | An id in the blockr option `assistant_models` |
| `base_url` | The blockr option `assistant_base_url`, with `assistant_api` |
| `api_key`, or `credentials` that give a key | The blockr option `assistant_api_key` |
| `params` | The model's settings ([The model's settings](#the-models-settings)) |
| `system_prompt` | A skill or a template ([The system prompt](#the-system-prompt)) |
| `echo` | Nothing, since no chat runs in R |

### A model that the browser cannot reach

A deployment sends every call to one base URL.
Some of the providers that ellmer reaches are out of a browser's reach:

- A provider whose API the assistant does not speak, such as AWS Bedrock, which `ellmer::chat_aws_bedrock()` calls.
- A provider that refuses calls from a page of another origin, such as Ollama's cloud.
- A model on a network that the server reaches and the visitor's browser does not.

A deployment reaches such a model through a gateway, such as OpenRouter, at `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`, or through a company's own proxy.
The base URL of the gateway or the proxy goes in `assistant_base_url`.
A proxy that needs no key from the page takes `"none"` in `assistant_api_key`.
A gateway also takes the place of a `chat_function` list that mixes providers, since it reaches the models of many providers through one base URL and one key.

### The key in the page

In version 0.1, the deployment's key stays in R.
In version 0.2, it reaches the page, where any visitor who can use the assistant can read it.
A visitor who can run R could read the key in version 0.1 too, through a block that takes code, such as the subset block of blockr.core.
So where a visitor can run R, a key in the page only makes visible what the visitor could already read.
No visitor runs R where the blockr options `locked` and `lock_load` are both on, and no block is left open with `locked = FALSE`.
The notes of blockr.core describe these locks.
There, the key in the page is exposed as the key in R was not.
A deployment that must keep its key from such visitors holds the key in a proxy of its own.
The page then calls the proxy with no key, through `"none"` in `assistant_api_key`, and the proxy decides who may call.

### The pick of the model

In version 0.1, the board option `llm_model` holds the pick of the model, which the user makes in the dock's options sidebar.
In version 0.2, each conversation keeps its own pick, in the state of the assistant's plugin.
The user picks a model in the chat's footer, where the deployment offers more than one model or names none.
A conversation that nobody picked a model for talks to the default, which is the first model of `assistant_models`.
So a script that gave `llm_model` a value, as `new_llm_model_option("gpt-5.4-nano")` did, names that model first in `assistant_models`.
It drops the board option from the board's `options`.

## The model's settings

In version 0.1, a chat function sets the model's settings through the `params()` of ellmer, such as `params(reasoning_effort = "high")`.
In version 0.2, a YAML file gives the settings of each model, under the model's id.
The blockr option `assistant_model_settings` names the file:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
options(
  blockr.chat_function = function(system_prompt = NULL, params = NULL) {
    ellmer::chat_openai(
      model = "gpt-5.4",
      system_prompt = system_prompt,
      params = ellmer::params(reasoning_effort = "high", max_tokens = 32000)
    )
  }
)
```

In version 0.2, the file is `models.yml`, beside the script:

```yaml
gpt-5.4:
  thinking_level: high
  max_tokens: 32000
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
options(
  blockr.assistant_models = "gpt-5.4",
  blockr.assistant_model_settings = "models.yml"
)
```

The file takes these settings, which the section Model settings of `?new_assistant_plugin` describes in full:

- The setting `thinking_level` gives the level at which the model reasons: `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`.
  It takes the place of the `reasoning_effort` of `params()`, at the level of the same name, and `off` takes the place of `none`.
  A model that reasons and has no level in the file reasons at `medium`, but for one case on OpenAI's Chat Completions API, which the help page gives.
- The setting `max_tokens` gives the most tokens that each call asks for the reply, as the `max_tokens` of `params()` does.
- The setting `context_window` gives the tokens that the model's context window holds, which sets when compaction runs ([Compaction](#compaction)).
- The settings `reasoning` and `images` say whether the model reasons and whether it takes images.
- The setting `like` names a model of the catalogs of pi, the library that runs the assistant's turns.
  The model then takes the settings of that model wherever the file gives none.
  This suits a model that a proxy serves under a name of its own.

The other settings of `params()`, such as `temperature` and `seed`, have no counterpart.

## Compaction

In version 0.1, the assistant compacts a conversation once the tokens of its last exchange pass the board option `chat_compact_tokens`.
That board option is `Inf` by default, which leaves compaction off.
A compaction keeps the last `chat_compact_keep` turns, 8 by default, and puts a summary in place of the older ones.
The blockr options of the same names give the defaults of the two board options.

In version 0.2, both board options go, with their blockr options.
The assistant compacts a conversation before each call to the model, as the CLI of pi does.
Where the tokens that the call would send pass the model's context window less 16,384 tokens, a call of the assistant's own first writes a summary of the older messages.
The newest messages stay, up to a quarter of the window.
So compaction is always on, and a deployment sets when it runs through a model's `context_window` ([The model's settings](#the-models-settings)):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
options(blockr.chat_compact_tokens = 100000)
```

In version 0.2, the model's settings give it a window of 116,384 tokens, so that a call that would send more than 100,000 tokens is compacted first:

```yaml
gpt-5.4:
  context_window: 116384
```

Where the file gives no `context_window`, the window comes from the catalogs of pi or from the base URL's list of models, and is 128,000 tokens where neither gives one.

## The messages that a board keeps

The blockr option `chat_save_turns` carries over, with its default of 50.
In version 0.1, it caps the turns of each conversation that a saved board writes.
In version 0.2, it caps the messages of each conversation that the board holds, and a saved board writes what the board holds.
A message counts as one of the turns of version 0.1 did, so a value keeps its meaning.
The board keeps whole exchanges, each from a message that the user sent.
The plugin keeps the older messages in the browser's memory while the board stays open.

The option takes `-1` for every message, where version 0.1 took `Inf`, since R cannot send `Inf` to the browser:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.1
options(blockr.chat_save_turns = Inf)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
options(blockr.chat_save_turns = -1)
```

The environment variable `BLOCKR_CHAT_SAVE_TURNS` takes `-1` too.
A value other than `-1` or a whole number of 0 or more, `Inf` among them, fails every change of a conversation, and the plugin logs the error as a board opens.
Under `0`, the board holds no conversation, as a file of version 0.1 held none.
The plugin then keeps each conversation in the browser's memory alone, so a reload loses it.

## The other blockr options

The blockr option `assistant_tools` goes.
In version 0.1, it adds tools of the deployment's own, as `ellmer::tool()` definitions in R.
The loop in the browser cannot call an R function.
So a package that needs a tool of its own gives a plugin class that registers a command.
The model runs that command through the assistant's edit tool, as it runs the commands of blockr.core.

The blockr option `assistant_commit_timeout_secs` goes, since the assistant commits nothing.
The assistant's edit tool returns once the blocks that the edit changed are current, or once the user stops the turn.
The blockr option `assistant_block_tool_pool` goes with the tools for each block class that it capped ([A deployment's skills](#a-deployments-skills)).

The caps on what the assistant's tools give the model carry over, with their defaults:

| Blockr option | Default |
|---|---|
| `assistant_summary_max_chars` | 2000 |
| `assistant_state_max_chars` | 20000 |
| `assistant_state_value_max_chars` | 128 |
| `assistant_description_max_chars` | 1000 |
| `assistant_skill_description_max_chars` | 1024 |
| `assistant_skill_catalogue_max_chars` | 4000 |
| `assistant_board_section_max_chars` | 3000 |
| `assistant_eval_max_chars` | 16000 |
| `assistant_review_max_blocks` | 50 |
| `assistant_plot_render_px` | 768 |
| `assistant_plot_render_range` | 200 to 2000 |
| `assistant_plot_render_max` | 4 |

The blockr option `assistant_board_section_max_chars` caps the whole Board section, at 3000 characters by default, where version 0.1 caps each of its parts at 1500.
So a deployment that sets the option sets it anew, for the whole section.
Where the board does not fit, the Board section lists first the blocks that a call most likely needs, and counts what it leaves out.

Each blockr option of version 0.1 goes as follows:

| Version 0.1 | Version 0.2 |
|---|---|
| `chat_function` | The blockr options `assistant_base_url`, `assistant_api`, `assistant_api_key` and `assistant_models` ([Where the calls go](#where-the-calls-go)) |
| `chat_compact_tokens` and `chat_compact_keep` | The `context_window` of a model's settings ([Compaction](#compaction)) |
| `chat_save_turns` | The same blockr option, with `-1` in place of `Inf` ([The messages that a board keeps](#the-messages-that-a-board-keeps)) |
| `assistant_skills` | The same blockr option ([A deployment's skills](#a-deployments-skills)) |
| `assistant_tools` | A command that a package registers |
| `assistant_commit_timeout_secs` and `assistant_block_tool_pool` | Nothing |
| The caps above | The same blockr options |

The blockr options `assistant_base_url`, `assistant_api`, `assistant_api_key`, `assistant_models`, `assistant_model_settings` and `assistant_template` are new.

## The generics that write the board

In version 0.1, the generics `describe_block()`, `describe_board()` and `describe_stack()` write the board for the model, in R.
In version 0.2, the plugin writes the board in the browser, from the board that the browser holds, so the three generics go.
A package that gives a method of one of them drops the method.
The model reads a block class through what the class registers instead: its description, its guidance and the JSON Schema of its state.

The generic `describe_result()` stays, with the methods that packages give it.
R answers the assistant's request for the summary of a block's result through it.
The tool `get_block_result` and the review of an edit send that request.
A package registers a method as in version 0.1, such as with the roxygen tag `@exportS3Method blockr.assistant::describe_result`.

## Boards that version 0.1 saved

A board that an app of version 0.1 saved opens in version 0.2 once blockr.convert has turned its file into a JSON board, as the notes of blockr.core and blockr.dock say.
The conversion makes the assistant's plugin with `new_assistant_plugin()`, in place of the extension.
The panel of the assistant's extension becomes the panel of the assistant's plugin.
The plugin starts with none of the conversations that the file holds.
The conversion also leaves out a `system_prompt` that the file holds, and the values of the board options `llm_model`, `chat_compact_tokens` and `chat_compact_keep`, which are gone.

## A deployment's skills

A skill is a directory that holds a `SKILL.md`, whose YAML frontmatter gives the skill's `name` and `description`, as in version 0.1.
The blockr option `assistant_skills` still names the directory of the deployment's skills.
The keys `requires`, `user-invocable` and `disable-model-invocation` carry over, and so does the tool `read_skill`, with its `name` and its `file`.
Three things change: the classes that a skill names, the tools that its text names, and the skill `layout`.

### The classes that a skill names

In version 0.1, a skill names block classes in `blocks:` by the ids under which their packages register them, such as `filter_block`.
It names extensions in `extensions:` by their classes, such as `dag_extension`.
In version 0.2, `blocks:` names each block class by its registry id in full: the name of its package, a hyphen and its id, such as `blockr.dplyr-filter_block`.
The key `plugins:` takes the place of `extensions:`, and names each plugin class by its id in full, such as `blockr.dag-dag_plugin`:

```yaml
---
# blockr.assistant 0.1
name: filtering
description: How to filter the rows of a study's tables.
blocks: [filter_block]
extensions: [dag_extension]
---
```

```yaml
---
# blockr.assistant 0.2
name: filtering
description: How to filter the rows of a study's tables.
blocks: [blockr.dplyr-filter_block]
plugins: [blockr.dag-dag_plugin]
---
```

The functions `available_blocks()` and `available_plugins()` of blockr.core list the classes of the available packages.
Each row gives a class's package and its id, which make up the class's id in full:

```{r}
# blockr.assistant 0.2
blocks <- subset(available_blocks(), package == "blockr.core")
paste(blocks$package, blocks$id, sep = "-")
```

A block class that a script defines has its id alone as its registry id, as the notes of blockr.core say, so `blocks:` names it by that id.

A skill that keeps a key of version 0.1 raises no error, but the model no longer finds the skill where it should:

- A skill whose `blocks:` names `filter_block` names no class that the app offers, so no tool lists the skill.
  The catalogue of the system prompt leaves it out as well, since it names a class.
- Nothing reads the key `extensions:`, so a skill that names classes only there names none.
  The catalogue then lists it as a skill for every task.

### The tools that a skill names

In version 0.1, the tools that change the board stage each change, and the tool `commit` applies what is staged.
In version 0.2, the tool `edit` applies a list of commands at once, as one step that the user's undo can take back.
Each command is one that the app registers, by its id, such as `blockr.core-add_block`, with its args.
The tool `list_commands` lists the commands, and `describe_command` gives the args of one.
Once the blocks that the step changed are current, `edit` returns its review of them, of those that feed them and of those downstream.
So nothing is staged.
A skill that says to stage changes and commit them says to pass them to one call of `edit` instead, as a list of commands.

In version 0.1, a skill may say this:

> Stage `add_block` and `add_link`, then call `commit` and read its report.

In version 0.2, the skill says this instead:

> Call `edit` with the commands `blockr.core-add_block` and `blockr.core-add_link`, and read its review.

Each tool of version 0.1 goes as follows:

| Version 0.1 | Version 0.2 |
|---|---|
| `list_blocks`, `describe_block`, `get_block_state`, `get_block_conditions`, `list_links`, `list_stacks`, `describe_stack` and `list_block_types` | The tools of the same names |
| `describe_block_type` | The tool of the same name, which gives the class's guidance in full and the JSON Schema of the class's state. The schema gives each state arg's type and description, in place of the `arguments` of version 0.1. The tool gives no example of an arg, and none of the worked examples that a class registered, each a complete state of its block |
| `get_block_result` | The tool of the same name |
| `inspect_results` | The tool of the same name, which binds the results of only the blocks that its `blocks` names, by their ids, where version 0.1 bound the result of every block. The result of a block that draws a plot is a `captured_plot` or a ggplot, which draws as it is printed, so the code `chart` draws the block `chart`, in place of `evaluate::replay(chart)` |
| `read_skill` | The tool of the same name |
| `add_block` | The command `blockr.core-add_block`. Where the new block has a link to it or from it, the command `blockr.core-add_link` adds the link, after `blockr.core-add_block` in the same call of `edit` |
| `remove_block` | The command `blockr.core-remove_block` |
| `modify_block` | The command `blockr.core-set_block` for the block's state, and `blockr.core-rename_block` for its name |
| `add_link`, `remove_link` and `modify_link` | The commands `blockr.core-add_link`, `blockr.core-remove_link` and `blockr.core-change_link` |
| `add_stack` and `remove_stack` | The commands `blockr.core-add_stack` and `blockr.core-remove_stack` |
| `modify_stack` | The command `blockr.core-change_stack` for the stack's blocks, and `blockr.core-rename_stack` for its name |
| The tools `add_<type>` and `modify_<type>` for each block class | The commands `blockr.core-add_block` and `blockr.core-set_block`, whose `state` follows the JSON Schema that `describe_block_type` gives for the class |
| `commit` and `discard` | Nothing, since `edit` applies its commands at once, and nothing is staged |
| `list_board_options` | The tool of the same name, which gives the value of each board option that the board holds, and no `default` |
| `set_board_option` | The command `blockr.core-set_option` |
| `list_extensions` | The tool `list_plugins` |
| `describe_extension` | The tool `get_plugin_state` |
| `modify_extension` | The command `blockr.core-set_plugin_state`, or a command of the plugin's class |
| `list_views` | The tool `get_plugin_state`, for the plugin `blockr.dock-dock_plugin` |
| `validate_layout` | Nothing, since each command checks its args |
| `add_view` | The command `blockr.dock-add_view`, which takes the view's `grid` in place of its `layout`, and makes the new view active. Where the active view should stay, `blockr.dock-activate_view` follows it, for the view that was active |
| `remove_view`, `rename_view` and `set_active_view` | The commands `blockr.dock-remove_view`, `blockr.dock-rename_view` and `blockr.dock-activate_view` |
| `add_panel_to_view` | The command `blockr.dock-add_panel`, which takes no `size` |
| `remove_panel_from_view`, `move_panel` and `resize_panel` | The commands `blockr.dock-remove_panel`, `blockr.dock-move_panel` and `blockr.dock-resize_panel` |
| `focus_panel` | The command `blockr.dock-activate_panel`, after `blockr.dock-activate_view` where the panel's view is not the active one |

The tools `list_commands`, `describe_command`, `list_plugins`, `get_plugin_state`, `edit` and `undo_edit` are new.
The tool `undo_edit` takes back the assistant's last edit.

A skill that shows a call of `inspect_results` gives it the blocks that the code reads, by their ids:

> Call `inspect_results` with the code `unique(data$Species)` and the blocks `["data"]`.

The commands of blockr.dock name a panel as `{ "block": id }` for a block's card, or as `{ "plugin": id }` for the UI of a plugin, by the id of the plugin's class.
In version 0.1, the view tools named a block's panel by the block's id, and an extension's panel by the extension's name, such as `slides`.

The Board section changes with the tools, and a message of the app's after the conversation's last message holds it, in place of the system prompt.
A block whose state is not valid yet reads `invalid`, where it read `unset` in version 0.1, so a skill that names the status `unset` names `invalid`.
No arg carries the mark `*` of version 0.1, which marked the args that `modify_block` could change.
A skill drops what it says of that mark.
The links into each block are on the block's line, in place of a list of the links.
The app's plugins and the board options are in the system prompt, in place of the Board section.
So a skill that sends the model to the Board section's list of links, of extensions or of options sends it to the blocks' lines, to the tool `list_links`, or to the plugins and board options in the system prompt.

### The skill `layout`

In version 0.1, blockr.assistant gives the skill `layout`, which teaches the view tools.
In version 0.2, blockr.dock gives a skill of that name, which teaches the dock's commands, in every app that runs the dock.
So a skill that sends the model to `read_skill("layout")` for the views keeps doing so.
It may drop what it repeats of the view tools, since the skill of blockr.dock teaches the commands that replace them.

## The functions that go

The table gives each function of version 0.1 that is gone, with what takes its place.

| Version 0.1 | Version 0.2 |
|---|---|
| `new_assistant_extension()` | `new_assistant_plugin()`, which a script calls only to place the assistant's panel or to give its conversations |
| `default_system_prompt()` | A template that the blockr option `assistant_template` names, or a skill |
| `describe_block()`, `describe_board()` and `describe_stack()` | Nothing, since the plugin writes the board in the browser |
| The `new_llm_model_option()` of blockr.core | The blockr option `assistant_models` |

The generic `describe_result()` stays, with its methods.
The function `new_assistant_plugin()` is new.
